results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice exhibit normal otolith organ zonal organization with unchanged striolar surface area and hair cell density in both utricle and saccule compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C21-C24, and C27 collectively demonstrate that loss of GPR156 does not affect macular patterning. The data in Figure 1B-C show quantitative measurements with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U test) confirming no significant differences in striolar organization between mutants and controls.

results.result: Type I and Type II hair cell numbers are preserved across all zones (LES, striola, MES) in Gpr156 mutant otolith organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C25-C27 are supported by immunolabeling data in Figure 1D-I using SPP1 and SOX2 markers with two-way ANOVA statistical analysis. The quantification shows no significant differences in hair cell type distribution between mutants and controls across all zones.

results.result: Mechano-electrical transduction properties are normal in lateral extrastriolar (LES) hair cells of Gpr156 mutant mice, with no differences in peak MET current, displacement sensitivity, operating range, or adaptation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C28-C31 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological recordings in Figures 2-4. The data show ~70% of LES HCs responded to stimulation regardless of genotype, with no significant differences in Boltzmann parameters (Gmax, X1/2, dx), operating range (~800-900 nm), or adaptation rates between mutants and controls.

results.result: Voltage-gated K+ conductances characteristic of Type I and Type II hair cells are preserved in Gpr156 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 3 showing that the distinctive electrophysiological properties of Type I HCs (large gK,L at rest, low input resistance ~50 MΩ) and Type II HCs (smaller voltage-gated conductance, higher input resistance ~500 MΩ) are maintained in mutants.

results.result: Hair cells in striola and MES zones show no systematic differences in electrophysiological properties despite Gpr156 expression throughout the maculae.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 acknowledge that while Gpr156 is transcribed in all HCs, no striking systematic differences were observed in striola and MES zones. However, the authors explicitly note low statistical power (Supplementary file 4), making it uncertain whether subtle effects exist.

results.result: In zebrafish lateral-line neuromasts, gpr156 mutants lack the functional asymmetry between hair cell populations, with all HCs showing mechanosensitive responses comparable to Emx2-negative (anterior-sensing) cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C40-C42, C71, and C73 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5. The data show that mechanosensitive GCaMP6s responses in gpr156 mutants are significantly larger than control A-to-P HCs (p=0.0043) and comparable to control P-to-A HCs, demonstrating loss of functional asymmetry.

results.result: Afferent receptive fields and orientation-selective innervation patterns are preserved in mouse Gpr156 mutant utricles despite loss of the line of polarity reversal.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C44-C51 are supported by dye-filling experiments (Figure 6) and Advillin-Cre genetic labeling (Figure 7). The data show that dimorphic afferents maintain normal terminal arbor organization, respect zonal boundaries, and selectively innervate HCs based on orientation (not HC orientation per se) in mutants.

results.result: In zebrafish neuromasts, afferent fibers maintain high selectivity for Emx2-positive or Emx2-negative hair cells in gpr156 mutants, independent of hair cell orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C101-C104 are supported by single afferent fiber labeling in Figure 9. Quantification shows that afferents in gpr156 mutants contact similar numbers of HCs per neuromast (p=0.48) and maintain high selectivity (control: 85.06±4.32%, gpr156: 81.29±3.17%, p=0.48) based on Emx2 expression despite all HCs responding to anterior flow.

results.result: Synaptic pairing is normal in gpr156 mutant zebrafish neuromasts, with no increase in unpaired pre- or post-synapses, contrasting with emx2 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by immunolabeling data in Figure 10. The data show complete synapses are unchanged across genotypes, while emx2 mutants show significantly more unpaired synapses (presynapses p=0.02, postsynapses p<0.0001) but gpr156 mutants do not (presynapses p=0.29, postsynapses p=0.12).

results.result: Afferent firing patterns and excitability are preserved in LES afferents of Gpr156 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by current-clamp recordings in Figure 8. Both control and mutant LES afferents showed similar current thresholds (~100 pA) and sustained firing patterns at 3×Ithresh (~95% of afferents), indicating normal ion channel expression and excitability.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice show no overt vestibular dysfunction in basic postural and balance tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C77-C79 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 11 and supplements. Mutants showed normal performance on balance beam, tail hanging, air righting, and contact inhibition tests, with no circling or head tremor behaviors at rest.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice exhibit severe swimming deficits characterized by underwater tumbling and inability to maintain upright posture, requiring significantly earlier rescue than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C55-C57, and C87 are supported by swimming test data in Figure 11B showing significantly reduced time to rescue in mutants (17.4±2.7s) compared to controls (49.9±3.0s, p<0.0001). This represents a major otolith-dependent behavioral deficit.

results.result: Semicircular canal-driven vestibular reflexes (VOR in dark and light, OKR, VOR adaptation) are normal in Gpr156 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by comprehensive VOR and OKR testing in Figure 12A-F and supplement. Both genotypes showed comparable gain and phase responses across frequencies, normal OKR confirming no visual deficits, and similar VOR motor learning capacity.

results.result: Gpr156 mutants show impaired otolith-mediated steady-state OVAR responses with significantly reduced bias, while transient canal-mediated responses remain normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C63-C66 are supported by OVAR testing in Figure 12G-H. Transient responses were comparable between genotypes, but steady-state bias was significantly reduced in mutants (0.039±0.26) compared to controls (3.85±0.54, p=4.03E-5), demonstrating specific otolith dysfunction.

results.result: GPR156 acts downstream of EMX2 to relay hair cell orientation and transduction information but not afferent selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 and C89 represent the main conclusion supported by the combined mouse and zebrafish data. Loss of GPR156 prevents HC orientation reversal (Figures 1-2), affects mechanosensitivity in zebrafish (Figure 5), but preserves afferent selectivity in both species (Figures 6-10).

results.result: Hair cell orientation is controlled independently from other zonally differentiated properties, and afferent segregation depends on EMX2 but not GPR156 or HC orientation per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C90-C92, and C112 are supported by the demonstration that Advillin-positive neurons segregate with HC orientation in controls but maintain segregation in Gpr156 mutants despite loss of orientation reversal (Figure 7), indicating EMX2 uses different effectors for orientation versus afferent patterning.

results.result: Zebrafish Emx2 may act through Gpr156 to impact Tmc2a/2b mechanotransduction channel function.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is speculative and based on inference from the functional data. While the loss of functional asymmetry in gpr156 mutants suggests GPR156 affects Tmc channel function, the mechanism is not directly tested and remains hypothetical.

results.result: Gpr156 mutants show more severe swimming deficits than Emx2 mutants, potentially because aberrant vestibular signals are more deleterious than absent signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 and C94-C98 compare behavioral phenotypes across models but rely heavily on speculation. While the swimming differences are documented, the explanations for why Gpr156 mutants are more severely affected (properly relayed but aberrant signals vs. absent/dampened signals) are not directly tested.

results.result: The Gpr156 mutant model is well-suited to specifically interrogate how HC orientation reversal influences vestibular function because it lacks confounding afferent patterning defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 and C113 represent a methodological conclusion supported by the comprehensive characterization showing that Gpr156 mutants have isolated defects in HC orientation without affecting afferent selectivity, HC numbers, or electrophysiological properties, making it a cleaner model than Emx2 mutants.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mouse otolith organs retain normal zonal organization, striolar surface area, hair cell density, and type I/II hair cell distribution across all zones (LES, striola, MES) in both utricle and saccule, despite loss of hair cell orientation reversal.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with one stating the study provides 'convincing evidence that mutant hair cells with abnormal, reversed polarity...retain wild-type localization' and another noting 'many features of hair cell function are preserved in the mutants-such as development of the mechanosensory organs.' The anatomical preservation is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice show normal mechano-electrical transduction (MET) properties in hair cells across all zones, including normal Boltzmann parameters, operating range, adaptation kinetics, and voltage-gated currents, with no systematic differences between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this finding. One reviewer states the study is 'exceptional in including...electrophysiological properties' and notes 'mutant hair cells of murine maculæ display essentially normal mechanoelectrical transduction and adaptation-with two or even three kinetic components-as well as normal voltage-activated ionic currents.' Another reviewer confirms the study provides 'convincing evidence' of 'mechanoelectrical transduction...properties' being retained.

results.result: In zebrafish gpr156 mutants, the functional asymmetry in mechanosensitive responses between Emx2+ and Emx2- hair cells is lost, with all hair cells showing larger responses comparable to wild-type Emx2- (anterior-sensing) cells, indicating that the EMX2-GPR156 pathway controls both orientation and mechanosensitive properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this zebrafish finding as part of the overall evidence. One reviewer notes 'there are a few key changes' including that 'the magnitude of responses of all hair cells to water flow resembles that of the wild-type hair cells that respond to flow arriving from the tail' and that this 'suggests that the Emx2-GPR156 signaling axis also impinges on hair cell mechanotransduction.' The data is treated as convincing evidence for the mechanosensitive role of GPR156.

results.result: Loss of GPR156 does not affect orientation-selective afferent innervation patterns in either mouse utricle or zebrafish neuromasts. Afferents maintain normal selectivity for hair cells based on Emx2 expression rather than hair cell orientation, with normal receptive field organization and synaptic pairing preserved in mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding. One states the study 'demonstrates that the bimodal pattern of afferent nerve projections in this organ is not causally related to the bimodal distribution of hair-bundle orientations, as also confirmed in the zebrafish lateral line.' Another reviewer notes this shows 'hair-cell orientation is not the feature that determines synaptic selectivity' and that 'the process of Emx2-dependent synaptic selectivity bifurcates downstream of Gpr156.' This is treated as a major conceptual advance.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice show no overt vestibular dysfunction in standard behavioral tests including balance beam, tail hanging, air righting, contact inhibition, and vestibulo-ocular reflexes (VOR) in dark and light, as well as optokinetic reflex (OKR) and VOR adaptation, indicating normal semicircular canal function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as evidence of 'mild behavioral dysfunction' overall. One reviewer notes the mutants 'exhibit normal posture and balance' and another states the study shows 'vestibular deficits in each model are relatively mild (normal balance beam, VOR and OKR).' The preservation of canal-driven responses is not questioned.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice demonstrate severely impaired swimming performance, characterized by underwater tumbling, inability to maintain upright posture, and significantly reduced time to rescue (17.4s vs 49.9s in controls, p<0.0001), indicating GPR156 is required for vestibular function during swimming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this behavioral deficit without challenge. One states mutants 'display defects in swimming behavior' and the finding is treated as part of the evidence for 'mild behavioral dysfunction' that is otolith-specific. The swimming deficit is accepted as a genuine consequence of loss of hair cell polarity reversal.

results.result: Gpr156 mutant mice show significantly impaired steady-state off-vertical-axis rotation (OVAR) responses with reduced bias (0.039±0.26 vs 3.85±0.54 in controls, p=4.03E-5), while transient OVAR responses remain normal, indicating altered otolith-mediated but not canal-mediated vestibular function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as evidence of otolith-specific deficits. One notes 'their vestibulo-ocular reflexes are perturbed' and the OVAR result is treated as convincing evidence that 'the absence of HC reversal...alters otolith-mediated OVAR responses.' The distinction between preserved transient and impaired steady-state responses is not questioned.

results.result: GPR156 acts downstream of EMX2 to relay hair cell orientation and transduction information, but not afferent selectivity, indicating that EMX2 regulates these features through separate effector pathways with GPR156 controlling orientation/mechanosensitivity and other effectors controlling innervation patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this conclusion. One states the study 'demonstrates that the bimodal pattern of afferent nerve projections...is not causally related to the bimodal distribution of hair-bundle orientations' and another notes it shows 'the process of Emx2-dependent synaptic selectivity bifurcates downstream of Gpr156.' A reviewer comments this 'establishes a framework for the following studies' to identify other EMX2 targets. This is treated as the central conceptual contribution.

results.result: Afferent firing patterns and excitability (current threshold for spiking ~100 pA, sustained spiking at 3×threshold) are unaltered in the LES of Gpr156 mutant utricles despite abnormal hair cell orientation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the comprehensive electrophysiological characterization. One notes the study includes 'firing properties of their afferent innervation' as preserved features. This finding supports the conclusion that afferent properties are independent of hair cell orientation and is not challenged.

results.result: In mouse vestibular epithelia, hair cell orientation is controlled separately from other zonally differentiated properties of hair cells or afferents, and vestibular deficits in Gpr156 mutants reflect the missing line of polarity reversal rather than defective neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly support this interpretation through their acceptance of the overall findings. One states the study 'demonstrates that the bimodal pattern of afferent nerve projections...is not causally related to the bimodal distribution of hair-bundle orientations,' which aligns with this conclusion. The logic connecting preserved cellular properties to behavioral deficits is not questioned.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support that macular patterning and hair cell localization are preserved in GPR156 mutants. OpenEval focuses on C5, C21-C24, C27 (striolar organization), while peer review covers C5, C21-C27 (including hair cell type distribution C25-C26). Both cite quantitative data with appropriate statistics showing no significant differences between mutants and controls.

OpenEval evaluates hair cell type distribution (C6, C25-C27) as supported by immunolabeling data. Peer review includes these claims (C25-C27) within their broader evaluation of preserved anatomical features. Both agree on the preservation of hair cell organization despite reversed polarity.

Both strongly support preservation of electrophysiological properties in mutant hair cells. OpenEval focuses on C7, C28-C31 (mechanotransduction and adaptation), while peer review covers C7, C28-C31, C33, C35, C74. Both cite comprehensive electrophysiological recordings showing normal transduction, adaptation kinetics, and voltage-activated currents.

OpenEval evaluates Type I and Type II hair cell electrophysiological properties (C32-C33) as supported. Peer review includes C33 in their broader evaluation of preserved electrophysiological features. Both agree these distinctive properties are maintained in mutants.

OpenEval rates C34-C35 as UNCERTAIN due to low statistical power for detecting subtle differences in striola and MES zones. Peer review includes C35 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of overall electrophysiological preservation. This represents a minor disagreement in confidence level regarding subtle regional differences.

Perfect agreement on zebrafish mechanosensitive calcium imaging data (C8, C40-C42, C71, C73). Both support that GPR156 loss causes all hair cells to show larger responses resembling wild-type posterior-to-anterior cells, demonstrating loss of functional asymmetry. Both treat this as convincing evidence for GPR156's role in mechanotransduction.

Both strongly support that afferent innervation patterns are preserved despite loss of hair cell orientation reversal. OpenEval focuses on C9, C44-C51 (dye-filling and genetic labeling showing maintained terminal organization). Peer review covers C9, C44-C51 plus additional claims about synaptic selectivity (C82, C90, C101-C104, C106, C108-C110, C112). Both treat this as a major finding showing orientation is not the determinant of afferent selectivity.

Both support that afferents maintain selectivity based on Emx2 expression despite altered hair cell function. OpenEval evaluates C10, C101-C104 (single fiber labeling showing similar HC contacts and high selectivity). Peer review includes C101-C104, C106, C108-C109 in their broader evaluation. Both agree this demonstrates afferent patterning uses different effectors than hair cell orientation.

Both support preservation of synaptic organization. OpenEval evaluates C105-C109 (immunolabeling showing complete synapses unchanged in gpr156 mutants vs. increased unpaired synapses in emx2 mutants). Peer review includes C106, C108-C109 in their evaluation of preserved afferent selectivity. Both agree this distinguishes gpr156 from emx2 mutants.

Both support that afferent firing properties are preserved. OpenEval evaluates C52-C54 (current-clamp recordings showing similar thresholds and firing patterns). Peer review evaluates C53-C54 as part of comprehensive electrophysiological characterization. Both agree afferent excitability is independent of hair cell orientation.

Both support that general balance and posture behaviors are preserved. OpenEval evaluates C11, C77-C79 (balance beam, tail hanging, air righting, contact inhibition all normal). Peer review includes C11, C77-C79 in their evaluation of 'mild behavioral dysfunction' with normal posture and balance. Both agree canal-driven behaviors are intact.

Perfect agreement on swimming test deficits. Both support C12, C55-C57, C87 showing significantly reduced time to rescue in mutants (17.4±2.7s vs 49.9±3.0s, p<0.0001). Both treat this as a major otolith-dependent behavioral deficit and genuine consequence of loss of hair cell polarity reversal.

Both support preservation of VOR and OKR responses. OpenEval evaluates C58-C62 (comparable gain, phase, and motor learning). Peer review includes C58-C62 in their evaluation showing 'normal balance beam, VOR and OKR.' Both agree canal-driven vestibulo-ocular reflexes are preserved.

Both support OVAR deficits as evidence of otolith-specific dysfunction. OpenEval evaluates C13, C63-C66 (preserved transient but reduced steady-state bias). Peer review evaluates C13, C64-C66, noting 'perturbed' vestibulo-ocular reflexes in OVAR. Both agree this demonstrates specific otolith dysfunction while distinguishing transient from steady-state responses.

Both strongly support the main conclusion that GPR156 mediates hair cell orientation reversal but not afferent selectivity. OpenEval evaluates C14-C16, C89 as the central finding. Peer review evaluates C14-C16, C89, C91, C99, explicitly stating this 'demonstrates that the bimodal pattern of afferent nerve projections...is not causally related to the bimodal distribution of hair-bundle orientations.' Both treat this as the major conceptual contribution.

Both support that EMX2 uses different downstream effectors for orientation versus afferent patterning. OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 (Advillin-positive neurons maintain segregation despite loss of orientation reversal). Peer review includes C91 in their evaluation of the bifurcation of Emx2-dependent processes downstream of Gpr156. Both agree this establishes a framework for identifying other EMX2 targets.

OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 regarding EMX2's bifurcated signaling. Peer review includes C90, C112 in their broader evaluation of preserved afferent selectivity. Both support that the process of Emx2-dependent synaptic selectivity bifurcates downstream of Gpr156.

OpenEval evaluates C67, C90-C92, C112 as supported evidence for bifurcated EMX2 signaling. Peer review includes C67 in their evaluation connecting preserved cellular properties to behavioral deficits. Both implicitly support the interpretation that different EMX2 effectors control different developmental processes.

OpenEval rates C72 (GPR156 affects Tmc channel function) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is speculative and based on inference rather than direct testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this mechanistic speculation about Tmc channels.

OpenEval rates C85-C88, C94-C98 as UNCERTAIN, noting the explanations for behavioral differences between models rely heavily on speculation. Peer review includes C87 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of swimming deficits. The disagreement is about confidence in mechanistic explanations rather than the behavioral data itself.

OpenEval rates C85-C88, C94-C98 as UNCERTAIN regarding comparative behavioral phenotype explanations. Peer review includes C85 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of 'mild behavioral dysfunction.' The difference reflects OpenEval's skepticism about mechanistic speculation versus peer acceptance of the overall behavioral characterization.

Both support that Gpr156 mutants provide a cleaner model than Emx2 mutants. OpenEval evaluates C99-C100, C113 as a methodological conclusion about isolated defects. Peer review includes C99 in their evaluation that the study 'establishes a framework for the following studies.' Both agree this model enables dissection of EMX2's multiple downstream pathways.

Peer review evaluates C67, C76, C84 regarding the logic connecting preserved cellular properties to behavioral deficits. OpenEval addresses C67 in R16 but does not have a separate evaluation specifically for C76 and C84. Peer review implicitly supports this interpretive framework through acceptance of overall findings.
